params.question: Which of the following preparation instructions primarily serves image quality rather than patient safety?

answers.text: Checking the eGFR before iodinated contrast injection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. eGFR assessment is a patient safety measure — it identifies kidneys vulnerable to contrast-induced injury, not an image-quality step.

answers.text: Asking the patient to drink water and avoid voiding before a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! A full bladder displaces gas-filled bowel from the pelvis, creating an acoustic window that improves visualisation of the uterus and adnexa.
Incorrect. MRI metal screening is a patient safety measure — ferromagnetic objects can become projectiles or cause tissue heating in the magnetic field.
Incorrect. Pregnancy exclusion before ionising radiation is a patient safety measure — it protects the foetus from radiation exposure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. A full bladder for transabdominal pelvic ultrasound serves image quality — it pushes gas-filled bowel out of the pelvis to open an acoustic window. eGFR checks, metal screening, and pregnancy exclusion are all patient safety measures.

Correct! A full bladder is an image-quality preparation. It creates an acoustic window by displacing bowel gas from the pelvis, allowing clear visualisation of pelvic structures. The other options — eGFR checks, metal screening, and pregnancy exclusion — are all patient safety measures.

params.question: A 62-year-old patient on metformin has an eGFR of 50 mL/min and is scheduled for a contrast-enhanced CT scan. What is the correct instruction regarding his metformin?

answers.text: Continue metformin as usual since the eGFR is above 30

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although eGFR above 30 means iodinated contrast can usually be given, metformin must still be withheld when eGFR is below 60 because contrast-induced kidney impairment could cause dangerous metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.

answers.text: Stop metformin 72 hours before the scan to clear it from the system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Metformin is withheld from the time of contrast, not before. Pre-scan withdrawal is not part of the protocol and has no evidence base for reducing the risk of lactic acidosis.

answers.text: Withhold metformin from the time of contrast and for 48 hours afterward, resuming only after renal review

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! When eGFR is below 60, metformin is withheld from the time of contrast for 48 hours and resumed only after confirming kidney function has not deteriorated.

answers.text: Switch permanently from metformin to insulin before the scan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A permanent switch is disproportionate. Metformin only needs a temporary hold — it is resumed after 48 hours once renal function is confirmed stable.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The correct protocol for a patient on metformin with eGFR below 60 is to withhold metformin from the time of contrast and for 48 hours afterward, resuming only after renal review confirms kidney function is stable.

Correct! For patients on metformin with an eGFR below 60, the protocol is to withhold metformin from the time of iodinated contrast for 48 hours, then resume only after confirming kidney function is stable. This prevents lactic acidosis if contrast-induced kidney injury occurs.

interactions.label: You hand a patient scheduled for a gallbladder ultrasound a written instruction

params.question: You hand a patient scheduled for a gallbladder ultrasound a written instruction sheet stating 'do not eat for four to six hours before the scan.' Which step should you take next to ensure she arrives properly prepared?

answers.text: Ask her to sign a consent form confirming she has read the instructions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A signed form confirms receipt but not understanding. Many patients sign documents without fully comprehending them — signing is not a substitute for verbal counselling.

answers.text: Provide the same written instructions to a family member as backup

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Preparation instructions must be communicated directly to the patient. Relying on a family member introduces a communication gap and does not confirm the patient's own understanding.

answers.text: Note the fasting instruction in the referral form and trust the patient to comply

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Noting the instruction in the referral is necessary for the radiology team but does nothing to verify the patient's understanding or likely compliance.

answers.text: Counsel her verbally on the fasting requirement and ask her to repeat the instruction back to you

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Verbal counselling paired with a teach-back check confirms the patient has understood the instruction. Written instructions alone do not account for literacy barriers or misunderstanding.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. After providing written instructions, the next step is to counsel the patient verbally and perform a teach-back check — asking her to repeat the fasting instruction in her own words. Written instructions alone are insufficient because they do not account for literacy or comprehension barriers.

Correct! Both written and verbal channels must be used together, followed by a teach-back check — the patient repeats the instruction in their own words. On the day of the scan, a door check confirms actual compliance. This matched approach is what makes preparation instructions safe and reliable.
